implementation_notes: In effect-oriented Scala the queue is a value: Queue.bounded[IO, A](capacity) makes offer fiber-blocking once the buffer is full and take blocking while it is empty, with synchronous, dropping, circularBuffer and unbounded as the other capacity policies - the bounded one is the load leveller, the dropping ones are shedders. Consumers are fibers (a worker pool is `take.flatMap(process)` repeated with bounded parallelism), so the queue bound, not the fiber count, is the control, and the same structure composes with resource-safe shutdown. Use it for new pure-FP code; the JUC queue remains appropriate when the consumer side is blocking Java interop.
pitfalls: Queue.unbounded has no bound, and dropping/circularBuffer policies discard elements - choose the capacity policy deliberately, because it is the pattern's core decision.
A fiber that both offers and takes from the same bounded queue can deadlock when the buffer fills; separate producer and consumer fibers.
Blocking JDBC or Thread.sleep inside an IO consumer starves the compute pool; wrap it with IO.blocking/interruptible.
Forgetting to terminate the worker fiber leaves the queue open and shutdown hanging.

variants.name: Pekko Streams Source.queue / BoundedSourceQueue with a throttled flow
variants.implementation_notes: Streams model the same pattern declaratively: Source.queue(bufferSize, overflowStrategy) materializes a queue that is fed by offer and drained by downstream demand, and the Pekko documentation recommends BoundedSourceQueue (a synchronous offer returning a QueueOfferResult) over the async-feedback SourceQueue when overload is expected, because asynchronous feedback can itself become the source of an out-of-memory condition. Combining the queue with throttle and mapAsync(parallelism) turns the drain rate into an explicit, declared number, which is the load-levelling contract in one place. Use this when the whole pipeline is already a stream graph; keep cats-effect or JUC queues for imperative consumers.
variants.code_sketch:
val (queue, done) = Source
  .queue[Job](1000, OverflowStrategy.backpressure)   // bound + explicit full-policy
  .throttle(200, 1.second)                          // steady drain rate
  .mapAsync(8)(process)                             // consumer concurrency
  .toMat(Sink.ignore)(Keep.both)
  .run()

queue.offer(job)   // feedback: Enqueued/Dropped/Failure/QueueClosed
pitfalls: OverflowStrategy.dropNew/dropHead are shedding; choosing them for work that must not be lost turns the pattern into its anti-pattern.
The async-feedback SourceQueue can accumulate pending offers faster than they are acknowledged - the documented reason BoundedSourceQueue exists.
throttle/mapAsync must be tuned together: a large mapAsync parallelism re-creates the overload at the downstream dependency.
